conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like to check in with you using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week so we can be sure you’re getting the right support in these early postpartum days. Everything you share stays between us, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. Ready to start?

First, I’m wondering:  
In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

It’s been a little tough. I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny—like when my husband made that silly face to get the baby to smile—but it takes more effort than it used to. Mostly I’m just tired, so even things that should feel funny sometimes fall flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly yes, I guess. I can still laugh—maybe not as easily as before the baby, but yes, I’ve found things funny a few times this week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes. I’ll catch myself looking forward to little stuff—like the baby’s bath time when he actually smiles—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. A lot of days I just think, “I hope I can get through this,” instead of really anticipating anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times. Like yesterday when he wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not swaddling tight enough or I missed his sleepy cue. My head knows babies just fuss, but I still felt like it was my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little, yeah. Most of it’s about the baby—like I’ll lie down and suddenly wonder if he’s breathing, so I have to check the monitor again even though I just looked. It’s not constant, but it pops up a few times a day without any real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—more like a quick wave of “what if something’s wrong?” than a full-on scare. It passes once I peek at him or pace the hallway for a minute, but it’s not an everyday thing.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes. There are stretches—especially in the late afternoon when I’m running on little sleep and he won’t nap—where I feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll think, “How am I going to keep doing this?” but then my husband walks in or the baby finally sleeps, and the pressure eases. So yeah, it piles up, but I haven’t felt totally swamped.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do have trouble sleeping, but it’s more because I’m listening for every squeak from the bassinet or running through to-do lists in my head. I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy I can’t sleep—it’s more that I’m wired and worried than truly miserable.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had moments—usually when I’m alone feeding at 3 a.m.—where a wave of sadness hits and tears just show up. It’s not all day, and it lifts when the sun comes up or when the baby smiles, but yeah, I’ve felt pretty low off and on this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not that extreme. I’ve teared up a couple of times, but I haven’t had those deep, can’t-stop kind of cries—just quick, quiet ones that pass.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt like a bit of an uphill climb: laughing takes more effort, excitement is muted, you sometimes blame yourself when your baby won't settle, and waves of worry or late-afternoon <sym>sadness</sym> catch you off guard. Even so, you still find moments of joy in your baby's smiles and in your husband's support, and you've had no thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 13, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional enjoyment and diminished excitement, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a couple of times" with specific examples, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>The mother describes recurring, intrusive worries about the baby's safety that arise "a few times a day" without an external trigger, aligning with "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, noticeable sadness that occurs "off and on" and brings tears, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 13 places you above the 12-point cutoff where <med>postpartum depression</med> becomes likely. You endorse <sym>anhedonia</sym>, frequent self-reproach, <sym>anxiety</sym> focused on infant safety, and tearful spells-symptoms that overlap with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Your description of feeling overwhelmed yet able to rally when support arrives suggests moderate but notable distress. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next 1-2 weeks to review these results
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health therapist</med> or support group; cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy can be very effective
3. Continue leaning on your husband or other trusted adults for practical help; even short naps or breaks reduce <sym>stress</sym> and improve mood
4. Practice good <med>sleep-hygiene</med>: dim lights before bed, limit screen time during night feeds, and consider alternating night shifts with your partner
5. Use brief self-check-ins each evening; if low mood, worry, or crying spells worsen, or if you ever have thoughts of self-harm, contact your provider the same day or call emergency services
6. Schedule a re-screen (EPDS, PHQ-9, or GAD-7) in 2-4 weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]  Clinician: [name], LCSW  

Symptoms / Concerns endorsed:  
- Mild anhedonia (reduced enjoyment, anticipatory pleasure)  
- Transient tearfulness / sadness, worse at night  
- Excessive self-blame regarding infant care  
- Intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety without objective trigger  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems secondary to hyper-vigilance about infant and mental “to-do” lists  
- Episodic feeling of “treading water” or being overwhelmed, especially late afternoon  

Patterns / Risk indicators:  
- Mood: fluctuating low mood, situational crying, not persistent all-day depression  
- Anxiety: generalized worry plus specific perinatal features (breathing checks, monitor re-checks)  
- Coping: partially buffered by partner support and infant positive cues; no sustained impairment in basic functioning  
- Safety: no self-harm ideation; no intent or plan  

Screening significance:  
Subthreshold depressive and anxiety symptoms in postpartum period; meets some but not full criteria for Major Depressive Episode or Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Continue monitoring for escalation (daily sadness, functional decline, hopelessness) and consider standardized tool (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) at next visit.
